title: Mai Bhago, the woman who led
hookLine: she shamed the deserters and led them back to fight, and later served as the Guru's guard

lines: A SIGNED PAPER: NOT OUR GURU.
ONE WOMAN WON'T LET IT STAND.
cards: You are not our Guru, and we are not your Sikhs. That, in effect, is what the paper said. During the long siege of Anandpur, tradition says, a band of Sikhs from the Majha country reached the end of what they could bear.
Hungry and worn down, they asked to go home. The Guru let them, on one condition: that they put it in writing. Sikhs remember the paper as the bedava, the disclaimer.
They signed it and left. Back home in Majha, the news got around, and one woman in the region heard it and would not let it stand. Today: Mai Bhago.

teach.b: Tradition says Mai Bhago went to the men who had come home and shamed them. Not with a lecture about loyalty, but with a challenge: if they wouldn't stand by the Guru, she would go herself.
Some tellings say she offered them women's clothes: they could stay at home, and she would go in their place. It stung, and it worked.

teach.h: SHE RODE OUT AT THEIR HEAD.
teach.b: The men gathered again, and she rode out at their head to find the Guru. They found him, or rather they found his pursuers.
Near a pool of water at Khidrana, the band led by Mai Bhago met the imperial force that was chasing Guru Gobind Singh, and they fought. Tradition says the men fell, and Mai Bhago was wounded.
Then comes the part Sikhs tell tenderly. The Guru went among the fallen. One of them, Mahan Singh, was still alive.
The Guru held his head in his lap and asked what he wished for. Mahan Singh asked him to tear up the paper.

teach.h: THE GURU TORE UP THE PAPER.
teach.b: And tradition says the Guru took out the bedava and tore it up. The men who had signed themselves away were his Sikhs again. Sikhs call them the Muktas, the liberated ones, and the place became Muktsar.
Tradition says she stayed near the Guru, served as one of his guards, and traveled south with him to Nanded. But the heart of it is what she did at the start. She didn't write the deserters off.
She went to them and led them back.

how: Sikhs remember Mai Bhago and the Muktas at Sri Muktsar Sahib, where the Guru tore up the bedava, and her story is told as an example of courage and of bringing people back to the Guru.

games.why: tradition says she challenged them and rode out at their head. at Khidrana they fought, and the Guru tore up their paper.

practice: Bring to mind someone who drifted away, from a friendship, a team, a family table. Notice any paper you've signed in your head, they left, that's that, and picture the door still open instead.
What would one honest step toward them look like, with no scolding attached?

wordCard.voice: Mai Bhago. The woman of Majha who shamed the deserters, led them back to the Guru, and stayed on as one of his guards. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Mai Bhago; Mai is a respectful word for an older woman, a mother.

carryVoice: Your line: she led them back. Even a signed paper can be torn up. Day eight hundred twenty-nine, done.
